sec: Hypertension 2023 · definition, risk factors and pathophysiology

items.q: Fill up: The chapter defines blood pressure as the measurement of the ______ exerted by blood as it ______ through the arteries.
items.exp: The definition line reads force exerted by blood as it pulsates through the arteries, an arterial rather than venous formulation. (Book p976)

items.q: Assess the equation and its legend: I Systemic blood pressure is written as cardiac output multiplied by systemic vascular resistance. II The abbreviation SVR is expanded on this page as systemic venous resistance.
items.exp: Both statements describe the page: the product is CO x SVR, and the legend printed to the right does expand SVR as systemic venous resistance although the term used in the equation is vascular resistance, the usual expansion. (Book p976)

items.q: A 10 mmHg fall in systolic blood pressure is quoted as reducing the risk of coronary artery disease and of stroke death by which percentages?
items.exp: The two branches under the 10 mmHg fall give a 40-50% reduction in CAD risk and a 50-60% reduction in stroke death. (Book p976)

items.q: Match each head of the risk-factor tree with what is hung beneath it — 1) Stroke 2) Cardiovascular disease 3) A fall in SBP of 10 mmHg … A) Smoking, hyperlipidemia, diabetes and hypertension itself B) Hemorrhagic stroke, labelled the most important C) A 40 to 50% drop in CAD risk and a 50 to 60% drop in stroke death
items.exp: Stroke takes the single hemorrhagic entry marked most important, cardiovascular disease takes smoking, hyperlipidemia, diabetes and HTN, and the 10 mmHg fall carries the two percentage reductions. (Book p976)

items.q: The pathophysiology block explains why a sustained rise in cardiac output cannot maintain hypertension. Which step does NOT belong to that chain?
opts: Rise in renal interstitial hydrostatic pressure
items.exp: The chain runs from a sustained rise in CO to increased renal blood flow, then to a raised, not lowered, renal interstitial hydrostatic pressure and increased Na+ and H2O excretion, which is why it will not produce sustained hypertension. (Book p976)

items.q: Fill up: The bracket that gathers the raised interstitial pressure and the natriuresis together is labelled ______, and the page concludes that this mechanism ______ sustained hypertension.
items.exp: Pressure natriuresis is the labelled bracket, and the line in red reads that this pathway will not produce sustained HTN. (Book p976)

items.q: Assess the two arms of the pathophysiology tree: I SVR or PVR, not cardiac output, is called the main factor for hypertension. II Its mechanism is vascular remodeling with a fall in vascular diameter and a rise in stiffness.
items.exp: The right arm carries the main factor for HTN label and the mechanism box lists vascular remodeling splitting into reduced diameter and increased stiffness. (Book p976)

items.q: Why does the page place beta-blockers outside the preferred first line in modern practice?
opts: Their major action is to reduce cardiac output, which pressure natriuresis can compensate for
They raise SVR and worsen vascular stiffness
They block the renin-angiotensin system completely
They cause sodium retention through ENaC activation
items.exp: The CO arm ends with the note that a beta-blocker's major action is to lower cardiac output, and that this is not a preferred first line drug now, consistent with the page's argument that a fall in CO alone does not sustain hypertension. (Book p976)

items.q: What does the small note box drawn beside the risk-factor tree assert about hypertension and kidney disease?
opts: Only the arrow from kidney disease to hypertension is ticked, labelled secondary HTN, while the opposite arrow is struck through
Both arrows are ticked, describing a fully self-perpetuating cycle
Only the arrow from hypertension to kidney disease is ticked
Both arrows are struck through, denying any relationship
items.exp: The box crosses out the HTN to kidney-disease arrow and ticks the return arrow under the label secondary HTN, a shorthand for the point that renal disease is a cause of hypertension here; in clinical practice long-standing hypertension does also damage the kidney. (Book p976)

items.q: A 24-year-old with a high-output state from severe anaemia has a systolic of 138 mmHg that normalises after transfusion. Which element of this page's pathophysiology best explains the normalisation?
opts: Pressure natriuresis prevented the raised cardiac output from sustaining hypertension
Vascular remodeling had not yet reduced arterial diameter
Beta-blocker activity fell and restored resting tone
Renal interstitial hydrostatic pressure fell below normal
items.exp: The CO arm ends in increased sodium and water excretion under the label pressure natriuresis, and the page states plainly that a sustained rise in CO will not produce sustained HTN. (Book p976)

items.q: Which of the following is not one of the four heads hung under the major risk association with HTN?
items.exp: The tree runs from major risk association with HTN into stroke and cardiovascular disease, with the SBP reduction branch and its two percentages beneath; LVH appears later as a target-organ finding, not here. (Book p976)

items.q: In the pathophysiology tree, what is written as the fall in vascular diameter and what as the rise, both under vascular remodeling?
items.exp: Vascular remodeling splits into a downward arrow beside vascular diameter and an upward arrow beside vascular stiffness. (Book p976)
